items.title: The Body
items.reason: Oriol Paulo's Spanish morgue mystery is driven by an actual evidence trail rather than a generic crime premise. Across the complete film, the guard's unexplained flight and the missing corpse precede discovery of the TH-16 toxin and Alex's affair; increasingly targeted disturbances suggest Mayka might have survived; the private-investigator lead and the guard's account alter the working theory; police cannot substantiate the alleged mistress Carla's identity; and the recovered body and final identity/revenge disclosure decisively reframe the case. This supports substantial investigation and clue-puzzling, regular but not constant meaningful information, and stronger late plot reversals than continuous progressive revelation. The adversarial staging of clues, deliberate framing and psychological pressure are central. The bulk is claustrophobic questioning and manipulation rather than physical action. Critics disagree on the visual direction (precise atmospheric framing versus repetitive camerawork), and an independent review notes repetitive clue/interrogation cycles in the middle-to-late stretch and a questionable element of the payoff. The final explanation requires some suspension of disbelief; those limitations are reflected in cadence, pace and craft rather than hidden by the strong ending.

items.title: The Call
items.reason: Lee Chung-hyun's Korean two-timeline thriller repeatedly pays out information and changes its consequences across its entire 112-minute runtime. The phone/diary clues establish that Seo-yeon in 2019 is speaking to Young-sook in 1999; saving Seo-yeon's father transforms the present; the discovery of Young-sook's predicted death, the thwarted exorcism and subsequent murders reveal the escalating threat; disappearing people and the kidnapping of Seo-yeon's younger self convert a friendship into cross-time hostage warfare. Police records, a failed explosion trap, and the revelation about who caused the childhood fire create further changes in both strategy and understanding. The revised notebook and simultaneous past/present confrontations culminate in another timeline reversal, including a contested mid-credits twist. This is genuinely frequent progressive revelation, not merely frequent investigative activity: formal investigation is secondary to tactical phone calls, records research and the antagonist's repeated alteration of history. The violence and psychological cat-and-mouse are pronounced; romance, military themes and rule-bound games are not drivers. Reviews praise brisk overall progression, clear parallel timelines, claustrophobic photography and tension, but independently fault the final reversal for weakening established time-travel logic. Individual scenes sometimes take a measured pace despite the brisk narrative.
